clue.text: Bent, maybe from eating unfinished meal

indicators.note: eating means one word swallows another, holding it inside

parts.note: 'from' is an example of a part of speech that links nouns, so 'maybe' marks it as one instance of that class

indicators.note: unfinished tells us to drop the final letter of the word for the meal

parts.note: a dish is a meal or course

explanation.surface: Someone bent over their food, perhaps eating a meal they never got to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like a description of the eater, but it is the definition; 'maybe from' asks for the grammatical class 'from' is an example of.
explanation.definitionFit: A bent is a natural inclination or tendency, which is the same idea as a leaning towards something.

clue.text: Italian dish recipe, middle bit of liver in mayonnaise

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for recipe (Latin 'take')

indicators.note: in places the picked letter inside the sauce word

parts.note: aioli is a garlic mayonnaise

indicators.note: middle bit of picks out the central letter of the five-letter word liver

explanation.surface: A recipe for an Italian dish that calls for a bit of liver in mayonnaise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle bit of' takes V, the central letter of LIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small stuffed pasta parcels, a classic dish from Italy's kitchens.

clue.text: Lament putting up online crossword item

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: E stands for electronic, as in e-mail, so online
the grid is the pattern of squares in a crossword

explanation.surface: Someone moans about having to put a puzzle online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting up' turns EGRID round to give the letters in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral song is a lament for the dead, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: I'm surprised to enter very popular bit of London

indicators.note: to enter means the exclamation goes inside the word for very

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
oh is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A visitor is amazed to get into a trendy part of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very popular' reads as one phrase, but 'very' belongs to the wordplay and 'popular' to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a lively West End district of London famous for its nightlife, restaurants and theatres.

clue.text: Mineral found as earth cools off

indicators.note: off suggests things gone wrong or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A geologist notes a mineral that forms as the earth cools.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a feldspar, a common rock-forming mineral found in granite.

clue.text: Devilish play, thus regularly unrehearsed

parts.note: an imp is a small devil, a devilish creature
to romp is to play boisterously

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word thus

explanation.surface: A wicked piece of theatre, thrown together without rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes T and U from THUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done off the cuff, without preparation, is extempore: spontaneous rather than practised.

clue.text: Actually accepting instruction to take dead tissue

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: in fact means actually
R abbreviates recipe, Latin for 'take', the instruction heading a prescription

explanation.surface: A patient is told to take some tissue, as instructed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepting' puts R inside IN FACT; R is the old prescription heading meaning 'take'.
explanation.definitionFit: This medical term names an area of tissue that has died from loss of blood supply.

clue.text: State added words to book supporting Tyneside pop group

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means placed underneath what follows it

parts.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England, NE
Wham! was the 1980s pop duo of George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley
PS, postscript, is words added to a letter
to book is to reserve or hire

explanation.surface: A northern pop band adds some words in support of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'supporting' means coming underneath. Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the fifty states of the USA, in New England.

clue.text: What potty contains is a little extreme

definitions.text: What potty contains is a little extreme

parts.words: What potty contains is a little extreme
parts.note: potty holds the letters OTT, a short form of a phrase meaning extreme; so 'a little' of the answer is inside potty

explanation.surface: A child's potty holds something a bit excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: The three-letter abbreviation for this phrase sits inside 'potty', so what the potty contains is a small version of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Going beyond reasonable limits is excessive, an idiom for something outrageously extreme.

clue.text: Iron and tungsten are rare

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
W is the chemical symbol for tungsten (wolfram)

explanation.surface: A chemist observes that iron and tungsten are scarce metals.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are scarce or rare are not many in number.

clue.text: Small part of shop error — grape's etc gone off

definitions.text: Small part of shop error — grape's etc gone off

parts.words: Small part of shop error — grape's etc gone off
parts.note: the small mark in 'grape's' is the misplaced punctuation typical of fruit stall signs; 'gone off' plays on rotting fruit and on the mark going astray

explanation.surface: A fruit seller's grapes have gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the stray punctuation mark wrongly added to plurals, as on market signs reading 'grape's'; the 'small part' is that tiny mark.
explanation.definitionFit: This term mocks the common sign-writing error of a stray mark before a plural s, named after fruit sellers.

clue.text: United will feed Hodgson a striker

indicators.note: will feed means one word is put inside another, like food into a mouth

parts.note: Roy Hodgson, the former England football manager
united means made one

explanation.surface: A football report: Manchester United will supply the England manager with a striker.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's United is the football club, but here it simply means made one.
explanation.definitionFit: Wayne Rooney was a celebrated forward for Manchester United and England.

clue.text: New/old part of India, mostly concrete, exclusive location

parts.note: Goa is a state on India's west coast

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter

parts.note: concrete means real, actual

explanation.surface: A property listing for an exclusive spot in India built mostly of concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims REAL to REA.
explanation.definitionFit: A place that people are barred from entering is a forbidden zone, one that excludes them.

clue.text: See 11
See relevant record is given to business partner

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
Co is short for company, a business
a pal is a friend or partner

explanation.surface: A relevant record is passed to a business partner to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is not an instruction to look but a bishop's diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Things relating to bishops and their dioceses, or sees, are described with this adjective.

clue.text: Lead, with another one, around country

parts.note: a co-star shares a leading role with another actor
I is the Roman numeral for one
ca, circa, means around

explanation.surface: A lead actor and partner tour around the country.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Central American republic between Nicaragua and Panama.

clue.text: Advance from left or right

indicators.note: from left or right says the letters read the same in either direction

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A political advance from either wing of the party.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome; 'from left or right' is the only wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To put up money is to advance it, as a loan or stake.

clue.text: Goes to America, welcoming right breakfast there?

indicators.note: welcoming means taking a letter in

parts.note: 'git' is US dialect for go or get going, so goes there is gits

explanation.surface: A traveller heads to America and gets a proper breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there' points back to America: this coarse cornmeal porridge is a Southern US breakfast staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarsely ground boiled maize is a traditional morning dish in the American South.

clue.text: Figure to bury put outside empty grave

indicators.note: put outside means the first word goes around the second

parts.note: to inter is to bury

indicators.note: empty means remove the inside letters, keeping only the outer ones

explanation.surface: A body to be buried is put outside an empty grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty' leaves only a word's outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A whole number is a figure, a numeral with no fractional part.

clue.text: Monster taps letters on it low down

indicators.note: on means placed after, in an across clue

parts.note: it, in old slang, means sex appeal, SA
squat means short and low to the ground
taps are marked C and H for cold and hot

explanation.surface: A monster taps out letters on a keyboard down low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' is sex appeal, SA; taps carry the letters C and H.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigfoot, the legendary ape-like creature of North America, is a mythical monster.

clue.text: Protecting screen TVs originally used to broadcast

indicators.note: originally takes the first letter of the word
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A shielding screen that TVs once used for broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' gives T, which 'broadcast' mixes with USED TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman soldiers locked shields overhead in a tortoise formation, a protective screen against missiles.

clue.text: Being banished until, oddly, nothing wrong about it

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outer pieces go round the inner

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing
awry means wrong, amiss

indicators.note: oddly takes the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Someone is exiled until nothing is wrong any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes U, T, L from UNTIL, and 'about' has O and AWRY go round them.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the state of being declared outside the protection of the law, a form of banishment.

clue.text: Rope that woman takes in was knotted

indicators.note: takes in means holds something inside

parts.note: her refers to a woman

indicators.note: knotted means tangled, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A woman's rope was tied in knots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knotted' makes AWS from WAS, which HER 'takes in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick cable used for mooring or towing a ship is a heavy rope.

clue.text: A daughter I love beginning to say goodbye

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, O

indicators.note: beginning to takes the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A parent tells their daughter they love her as they start to say farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish farewell is used in English as a casual way to say farewell.

clue.text: Out cold, lifeless

indicators.note: lifeless says to remove a word for life or vigour, zing, from the word before

parts.note: freezing means very cold

explanation.surface: Someone knocked out cold, apparently dead.
explanation.walkthrough: Zing means life or zest, so 'lifeless' takes it from FREEZING. 'Out cold' looks like one phrase, but 'Out' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner who is out has been released, at liberty.

clue.text: One exemplified by 'good'

parts.note: e.g. means for example, so exemplified

explanation.surface: Something described as an example of goodness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is a person, as in calling someone a good or bad sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang calls a person a good or bad one of these, so it can stand for a chap.

clue.text: Arrogant nurses see proof?

indicators.note: nurses means holds closely, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: imperious means arrogant, domineering
v. abbreviates vide, Latin for see

explanation.surface: An arrogant nurse asks to see proof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'proof' is used as in waterproof; the question mark flags it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that cannot be penetrated is resistant, just as waterproof material keeps water out.

clue.text: A water feature's unlikely use, for instance

indicators.note: unlikely suggests an improbable arrangement, so the letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A garden fountain would be an odd thing to use, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'water feature' suggests a garden fountain; it is a physical property of water.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin-like effect at the top of a liquid, letting insects walk on it, is a property of water.
